title: The fire on the mountain
hookLine: on the way home Musa sees a fire and goes to fetch a coal, and is spoken to in the sacred valley of Tuwa
carry: you are in a sacred valley
tomorrow: The staff and the shining hand

cards: A trip out for milk. A wrong turn down a street you didn't know. A borrowed ladder carried back to a neighbor.
Errands are where a lot of stories start. Years have passed at Madyan. Musa has served his time and is traveling with his family, in the dark and the cold.
Off on the side of a mountain, he sees a fire. He tells his family: wait here. Maybe I can bring you back a burning coal, or find someone there who can show us the way.
He's going for a coal. That's all.

teach.h: O MUSA, I AM YOUR LORD.
teach.b: Surah Ta-Ha tells what happens when he gets there. He's called by name. O Musa.
So take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed. Before the mission, before the signs, the first instruction is about his feet.

Commentators have offered more than one reason: out of respect, the way you'd take off your shoes entering a home; or so he'd feel the holy ground directly, nothing between him and it. The Qur'an doesn't explain.
It just asks. Then the heart of it: I am Allah; there is no god but Me.
So worship Me, and establish the prayer for My remembrance. Before Pharaoh, before any rescue: who God is, and prayer.

This is why Musa has a special title in Islam: Kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to. Surah an-Nisa says Allah spoke to Musa directly. Surah al-Qasas adds that the voice came from a tree, on the right side of the valley.
Jews and Christians tell this moment too, as the burning bush in Exodus. Musa didn't climb that mountain looking for God. He was looking for a coal to keep his family warm, and directions home.
The sacred valley was right there on his errand. He just had to stop, and take off his shoes.

how: Muslims take off their shoes before entering a mosque or stepping onto a prayer space, and Musa is honored with the title Kalimullah, the one to whom Allah spoke.

o: the one who wrote down Allah's words
the one Allah spoke to directly
the one who ruled Egypt as its king

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Musa climbed the mountain looking for God
he went for a burning coal to warm his family, and maybe directions.
the first thing he's told to do is take off his sandals
you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.
the Qur'an explains why he had to remove his sandals
it doesn't. commentators suggest respect, or feeling the holy ground directly.

games.q: you're Musa, traveling at night with your family. you see a fire on the mountainside. what do you do?
o: keep moving. fires in the desert mean trouble.
tell your family to wait, and go fetch a coal.
send one of the family to see who's there.
games.why: he goes himself, hoping for a coal or directions, and is called by name: O Musa, I am your Lord. take off your sandals.

practice: Take your shoes off if you can, socks are fine, and stand on whatever floor you're on: carpet, tile, kitchen linoleum, grass. Feel it under your feet; don't try to make the room holy, just treat it for a while as if it might be.
If you pray, you can remember the words, there is no god but Allah; if not, simply stand, and let the ground be the ground.

wordCard.voice: Kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to: Musa's title, from the voice that called him out of the fire on the mountain.

orig.note: Arabic: "the one Allah spoke to," Musa's title in Islam, drawn from Qur'an 4:164.

carryVoice: Your line: you are in a sacred valley. It all started with a trip for a coal. Day forty-eight, done.

sources.ref: Exodus 3:1–6 (the burning bush, named as a neighbor)
